newsitem.title: FRANCE: Merged Suez-Lyonnaise must prove worth - analysts.
newsitem.headline: Merged Suez-Lyonnaise must prove worth - analysts.

text.p: The new merged utilities giant Suez Lyonnaise des Eaux will have to prove to investors that bigger is better, financial analysts said on Tuesday.

"Everything at the moment is speculative," said Dominique Carrel of CDC Bourse after Lyonnaise des Eaux and holding Cie de Suez outlined to analysts on Monday plans to form a global heavyweight in infrastructure services.

Analysts said the briefing was short on details about how the group would achieve ambitious goals that include a profit this year of more than 3.5 billion francs ($600 million), a doubling of profit per share in five years and 80 percent sales growth by 2001.
Lyonnaise, which is active in water distribution, construction and communications, had profits of 1.35 billion francs in 1996 while Suez had profits of 843 million francs.

"They never told us how they were going to achieve it (the profit rise)," said Carrel, expressing concern profit increases might be mainly through capital gains on disposals. "There are a lot of question marks," said Jean-Louis Gauchet of NSM bank.

Others were more confident about the deal which will draw on Lyonnaise's utilities skills and Suez's cash pile. "It's a very logical merger, giving the group the financial means to pursue its development," said Transbourse's Marie-Christine Linivec.

"I'm still very positive on the future of the new group," she said, predicting it would have "good quality" results. She said its control of Suez's Belgian energy and services company Tractebel was an added plus because of its international reach.
The group, whose merger goes before shareholders for approval on June 11, will focus on four core businesses -- energy, water distribution, waste management and communications.

Analysts said the new group would have to prove the value of the merger before its stock could outperform the blue-chip CAC-40 index of leading French shares. "The market will be divided until it sees some results," said Linivec.

And analysts said they wanted to know more about Suez Lyonnaise's strategy for building up its communications arm, which at the moment makes up just one percent of the combined group's 1996 pro forma operating profits.

The shares climbed on Monday following Friday's formal announcement of the proposed merger, but they slipped on Tuesday. Suez shares closed down 0.21 percent at 286 francs, and Lyonnaise's stock fell 1.29 percent to 534 francs.

The merger, which marks a major step in the consolidation of France's corporate landscape, will create a group boasting annual sales of 210 billion francs and a stock market capitalisation of 75 billion francs.
The merger should bring savings of 200 million francs and combined debt will stand at 46 percent of equity.

Its chief executive will be Suez chairman Gerard Mestrallet, who turned around Suez, aggressively shedding assets, after it racked up 8.7 billion francs in losses in 1994 and 1995. Jerome Monod, chairman of Lyonnaise, will head the supervisory board.

Under the deal, Suez shareholders will get 20 Lyonnaise shares in exchange for 41 Suez shares and a special dividend of 3.8 billion francs or 24.6 francs a share. Even with the payout, there will still be a big chunk of Suez's six billion franc cash hoard that can be used for Lyonnaise's expansion plans.

Analysts say many of Suez's banking and industrial assets are likely to be shed as non-core activities along with some of Lyonnaise's construction operations. But the new group insists there are no immediate sale plans except for disposal of some of Suez's small stake in glassmaker Saint-Gobain.
